entry.title: Learning to Triage Vulnerabilities and Their Real Product Impact — or How Product Security Turns a Finding into a Risk Decision
entry.summary: A practical playbook: triage → applicability → exposure → reachability → exploitability → blast radius → business impact → treatment → verification. When I was working in SecOps, one of the most useful lessons I learned was painfully simple: a red CVSS number or a “High Impact” scanner alert is not, by itself, proof of a real product risk. If the dashboard is screaming 9.8 in bright red, congratulations — you have a signal. The thinking part still belongs to you. A scanner can tell you that a vulnerability has a CVSS score of 9.8. An SCA tool can flag a vulnerable dependency. SAST can identify a potentially dangerous sink. DAST can confirm behavior in a running application. A CNAPP can surface a cloud misconfiguration. entry.title: Green Checks Lie: Backend Error Tracking for Cron Jobs, Workers, and Silent Web APIs
entry.summary: Short answer: use separate signals for an exception, a missed schedule, an unfinished run, and an invalid result. Exception capture is necessary for cron jobs, workers, and web APIs, but it cannot see work that never starts or output that is wrong while the process exits normally. That distinction is the starting point for an error-tracking design I can evaluate from a notebook through production. The simple approach is one try/except around each entry point. The more useful approach gives every run a lifecycle, checks the application contract, and sends searchable context without copying prompts or customer data into an incident system. Think in four questions: did execution start, did it finish, did code raise, and was the result acceptable? A scheduler heartbeat answers the first. A com…

entry.title: Catching Terraform Drift Early: Scheduled Plans in GitHub Actions with AWS OIDC (No Long-Lived Keys)
entry.summary: Terraform state describes what you think is deployed. Drift is the gap between that and reality: someone changes a security group in the console during an incident, an autoscaling event edits a tag, or a teammate runs apply from a stale branch. Drift is rarely dramatic on the day it happens. It hurts later, when an unrelated change produces a plan full of surprises and nobody is sure which side is right. The fix is cheap: run terraform plan on a schedule, read the exit code, and open an issue when something differs. This post builds that pipeline in GitHub Actions, authenticates to AWS with OIDC so there are no stored access keys, and fans out across multiple workspaces with a matrix. An IAM OIDC identity provider for GitHub and a read-only IAM role that only this repository's workflow can…
